title: 20 inch arms CMON (Hypertrophy Log #9)
summary: Training log covering a quick suitcase deadlift session, a Sunday arm/core/upper-back day, a lower day with SSB Bulgarian split squats and weighted neck work, and outdoor husafell-style carries and mace forearm work. He explains his cues for partial preacher curls, long-lever planks, tiger push-ups, side bends and rest-pause, and his upper/lower split.
claims: The more you put into anything in life, the more you get out of it
Heavy suitcase deadlift is not great for hypertrophy but is a good quick lift when he has only about 25 minutes to train
Cheap clamps let heavy plates tilt and slide on a one-arm implement once loads exceed about 200 lb; use proper clamps
He does suitcase deadlifts without straps until grip fails, then straps up immediately to finish reps
Suitcase deadlift barely taxes the low back, is grip-heavy, builds forearms and heavily works the obliques
His top suitcase deadlift set is a 3-rep max per side; left grip is slightly stronger, and he strapped up for a 4th rep
He does a partial 'preacher' curl using his own torso as the pad, stopping when the forearm is parallel to the floor, to lift more weight
Going deeper on that curl makes the shoulders move; keep shoulders back and frozen so the biceps alone lift the maximum load
He uses full range of motion bicep movements elsewhere; the partial curl is one specific tool, done for an 8-rep max
Heavy partial curls are not recommended for people new to bicep isolation as they can be dangerous; for him progress on it grew his biceps
Long-lever plank: on tiptoes, push hips, shoulders and head far forward with a weighted backpack sitting high on the torso so all stress goes to the core
Standard push-up-position planks put a lot of emphasis on arms and shoulders rather than the core
Hold long-lever planks 10-20 s and stop only when the elbows bend into a push-up position, which signals core failure
With 50 lb in the backpack the long-lever plank was very hard; a normal plank can easily take 100 lb
He is at 220 lb and maintaining, no longer gaining weight
Chest-supported style rows: grip slightly tilted (not pronated, supinated or neutral), rotate at the hip only at the bottom for more lat stretch
Standardize rows by requiring the weight to touch the chest; if it can't touch, the set is over, preventing body english
That more upright rowing variation hits the traps more than lats; a good builder for the whole upper back
He uses straps on rows only when he has no choice, usually not on the first set
Tiger push-up (tricep/sphinx push-up): elbows in but not perfectly tucked, pressing off the top knuckles like claws for wrist comfort and tricep focus
Giving exercises cool names makes you more excited to do them
Load tiger push-ups as heavily as possible and use a slow negative, as with JM presses, for elbow health
He does sets of 15 tiger push-ups; triceps were a lagging part and responded well
Dumbbell side bends: free hand behind head, end range when that elbow points at the ceiling, to stretch the whole core and obliques
Use a rolling (round-handled) dumbbell for side bends so it rolls off the leg comfortably
Side bends for sets of 15, finishing each rep with a slight crunch in and to the side
At 17-18% body fat his obliques still show separation; if you are leaner and your core doesn't look like that, isolate and train it seriously
Oblique training will not thicken your waist; it makes the physique look more aesthetic
Preacher-style curl with full pronation on a one-arm bar for reps of 12 with rest-pause
Rest-pause: at failure, rest at the bottom 15-20 s focusing only on the muscle (no phone), then squeeze out more reps
Rest-pause is especially valuable for advanced lifters, giving 10-20% more hyper-intense volume close to failure; prefer it over drop sets
Rest-pause has changed how he approaches isolation training
He achieved a good waist-to-shoulder ratio despite a big waist, so anyone can
He follows an upper/lower split: upper body 3x a week and lower body 2x a week
He abandoned dumbbell Bulgarian split squats as inferior for hypertrophy; do them on a Smith machine, with SSB, or on a belt squat
Set safeties high on split squats only to balance yourself, not to push off or cheat the negative
Bulgarian split squat tempo should be slow and controlled unless you are an athlete
Wearing Olympic squat shoes raises the heel and makes split squats more quad-biased
Place the front foot at the center of the squat rack for best balance once the back leg is elevated
He tapes his left knee when his previously torn patellar tendon flares; you can train legs with minor injuries if you're smart
He trains neck on every lower-body day so he never skips it
He is trap dominant; traps overshadow his lats
Bent-over neck harness extension while holding a bar with arms open makes it a compound upper-back and neck movement that hits mid/lower traps
Tiny isolation movements for the upper thoracic back are not very effective; train it in the way that feels most effective
Rest-pause on neck: deload the neck on the chains for 5-10 s, then continue; the first rep after should feel like hell
If post rest-pause reps feel easy, the weight is too light
Neck reps of 20; never go below 10 reps because the neck is fragile
On non-lifting days he does 20-30 min of outdoor weighted carries instead of resting; it gets him active and connected to nature
Proper Husafell stone carry (arms crossed, upper back squeezed) does little for hypertrophy; he holds it from the bottom like a pot with straight arms to load biceps and triceps
Carrying with extended arms after arm days makes the arms the limiting factor, not legs or cardio
Leaning the torso back during carries deloads the arms to get more trips while keeping arm tension
A 5 lb mace is all you need for forearm raising motions; a 20 lb mace is unusable for forearms
Mace work burns the brachioradialis and has been great for rehabbing his wrist; his work capacity is going up
